doc.title: Jackie Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Becoming a drummer and studying with Aubrey Brooks
summary: Childhood love of music in Harlem led him to a music school on Mount Morris Avenue where Aubrey Brooks taught him drums, rudiments and ensemble playing, culminating in a visit by Bill Robinson.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: How did you come to be a drummer?
I’ve been wondering that all my life.

I’ve been wondering about that. Well I guess I was always destined to be one I guess, although I like music, I was just infatuated with music for as long as I could remember from a kid. I was always, you know kids roll up paper and blow in it imitating a horn or they’d be beating on something. So I was always fascinated with music. I could remember — I liked almost every instrument I heard. And I could remember listening, staying up nights, you know, listening, with my ear glued to the radio listening to music. Because then, as I was growing up, they had music going on all the time you know. There was radio programs, you know they had bands on the radio. And well I grew up in New York and in Harlem there was always some place where music was being played. You know there was clubs. And so I guess I just migrated to the drums through hearing music, seeing other people play, and just having a little talent and initiative to pursue it. Because I do remember studying a little piano — a cousin of mine was studying piano — and I always used to like I said always dabble around with the keyboard and stuff like that, you know just by ear and things, picking out melodies. So I heard, through hanging out through the rest of the kids, they would have little schools, you know, where kids could go and study an instrument. So I remember one day in high school one of the kids came by and said, “Have you heard about this particular school on Mount Morris Avenue, they have a great school, guys go over and play.” And this particular guy I think he was playing and studying saxophone or something. And everybody was emulating the different musicians, you know like Max Roach or Lester Young or somebody. I said, “Gee I think I’d like to go over to check it out to see what’s happening.” So I went over there and I, you know, I was introduced to the teacher. His names was Mr. Brooks, I’ll

never forget him, Aubrey Brooks. And he gave all the kids a wonderful little like screening, you know, to see what talent they had. So I told him I would like to study some drums, you know. So he was showing me a few things. This is the pad, he started out with the pad and as time went on, we had the classes there, he taught the rudiments of music, you know, not only the drums he taught theory and all the scales and everything, which was so wonderful. And the school was really nice. Because it gave the kids an incentive, you know to have something to do rather than to be hanging out on the streets all the time. So that’s where I really got an interest in it you know. And he made it even more interesting by inviting certain celebrities from the theatrical world to come. He’d say well next week — or a couple weeks from now we’re going to have Bojangles, Mr. Robinson, you know. So Bill Robinson is going to come and I want you to have a nice program prepared for him. And so I say “what!” So we all were very enthusiastic. So he got a wonderful little drum choir like together for us. And we all had, all the people that were playing the drums filled in with percussion. He had somebody playing tenor drum, the snare drum, tambourine, whatever. You know he was very creative that way, and he would create rhythms and stuff. And we all had our parts you know. That’s the first time I ever was aware of playing an ensemble thing.
How they fit together. What’s the role.

Right. And how everybody was important you know. And Mr. Brooks put that thing together and we did it and Bojangles came, Bill Robinson came in and he spoke to us and he was so uplifting. You know he was so proud to see us. And we were proud to see him. And so he was so complimentary to all of us. And that was a real boost to us. And not only our class, but that particular school was good, it had vocalists, it had other instrumentalists, you know, violins and stuff like that. But just a wonderful school. So in the process of doing that, Aubrey Brooks said, “Well you know you’ve got to have a little extra time I’d like it if you get a chance,” because this is a school, “if you get a chance, one day I would like for you to come and study privately — you know I want you to kind of stretch your talent a little bit.” So I say okay Mr. Brooks, but you know, when I get a chance. And as time went on, I finished junior high and then I went to high school, and I was, I majored in art in high school. I didn’t go to music and art, you know, like most kids that wanted to — because I was into art also, you know like drawing and commercial art. So I studied but I think I was leaning toward the music. Because I would always be in the band room, you know, messing around with the drums and stuff. So finally the musical director of the high school, Mr. Klinger, he said, “Well why don’t you join the band since you’re in here all the time?”
